cmd/compile: assign inline cost 1 to byteorder loads and stores

On architectures with CanMergeLoads, hairyVisitor discounts calls to
encoding/binary and internal/byteorder load, store, and append functions
to cost 1 when computing a caller's inline cost. However, CanInline
still records each load and store function's full AST cost (17 to 67)
as its own Inl.Cost, even though they lower to combined loads or stores.
Call-site checks in inlineCostOK and inlheur score calls using that
uncombined cost, blocking inlining when the call-site budget is tighter,
such as in big functions or under call-site score penalties.

Set Inl.Cost to 1 in CanInline for the load and store functions on
CanMergeLoads targets so caller budgeting and call-site checks agree.
The append functions keep their measured cost (9 to 33) since they
inline to a capacity check and growslice slow path around the store,
while keeping their caller-side discount in hairyVisitor.

No change in generated code for std and cmd. On

fix(types): don't constrain component $el type to Element (#15040)

`$el`'s type param (`TypeEl`) lives in `@kullanici/runtime-core`, which is
renderer-agnostic, yet it's constrained to the DOM `Element` interface.
Custom renderers (TUI, canvas, native, …) have host nodes that aren't DOM
`Element`s, so they can't type `$el` without laundering through `& Element`.

Relax the `TypeEl` bound to unconstrained (default stays `any`): DOM
elements still qualify, non-DOM host nodes now do too. Backward compatible —
it only widens accepted inputs.

simd/archsimd: add InterleaveLo/Hi and ConcatEven/Odd on SVE

This adds InterleaveLo, InterleaveHi, ConcatEven, and ConcatOdd on SVE
integer types, with the same names and meanings as the NEON operations.
They map directly to ZIP1, ZIP2, UZP1, and UZP2.

This also adds them to spec, marked //specgen:experiment. The existing
declarations of these operations already match the spec semantics:
InterleaveLo/Hi and ConcatEven/Odd on NEON integer vectors, and
InterleaveLo/Hi on amd64 128-bit integer vectors (VPUNPCKL*/VPUNPCKH*).
At 128 bits, the whole vector is a single lane, so these agree with the
whole-vector meaning, and the existing tests check all of them against
the same reference functions. amd64's wider forms are the separate
InterleaveLo/HiGrouped operations, which work within each 128-bit lane.
These declarations now get their docs from spec.

The next CL adds HiToLo on all targets, and its SVE implementation is
built from InterleaveHi and ConcatEven.

simd/archsimd/_gen/specgen: match gofmt indentation in reshapeDiagram

reshapeDiagram previously prefixed each line with "\t  " (a tab followed
by two spaces). Because every line of the preformatted block shared two
leading spaces after the tab, go/format (format.Source) stripped those
two spaces down to "\t" when formatting generated Go files.

Emit "\t" directly from reshapeDiagram so specgen.FormatComment produces
gofmt-canonical output. This avoids a redundant edit-and-reformat cycle
in specdoc.Fill and allows cmd/specstats to recognize all 96
ReshapeToUint* declarations as spec-sourced.

cmd/compile: mark the x86 SBB carry-mask ops as clobbering flags

SBBQcarrymask and SBBLcarrymask (AMD64Ops.go, 386Ops.go) expand to an SBB
instruction, which writes the flags register, but their OpcodeTable entries
do not set clobberFlags, unlike the borrow-taking SBBQ/SBBL/SBBLconst forms.

The lowering of an unbounded shift emits CMPQconst [width] count feeding the
count mask. When the program also compares the count against the same width,
the comparison's SETcc shares those flags; flagalloc believes they stay live
across the SBB, and the assembler can place the SBB between the CMP and the
SETcc, which then reads the SBB's flags. The compiled condition for
"y == 64" is "y >= 64":

	func f(x, y uint64) uint64 {
		r := x << y
		eq := uint64(0)
		if y == 64 {
			eq = 1
		}
		return r + eq
	}
	// f(1, 65) returns 1; the spec says 0.

The same wrong code affects y != 64 (compiled as y < 64), unsigned and
signed right shifts, the 32-bit form (y == 32), and on 386 a decomposed

simd/archsimd: document platform dependence of float ReduceMax and ReduceMin

Like Max and Min, the handling of NaN and signed zeroes by ReduceMax and
ReduceMin on floats may vary by platform. Point to Max and Min for the
details.

Today, only arm64 implements float ReduceMax and ReduceMin, and it
follows IEEE 754-2019, which agrees with Go's max and min, so spec does
not yet model any platform variation.

Use uniforms in the Porter Duff blend shader instead of specialization constants (#195458)

Changes the Porter Duff blend shader to use uniforms instead of
specialization constants for the blending coefficients. As each
specialized variant triggered a full shader compile, this removes 14
shader compiles (~23%) from the engine initialization path, it also
removes overhead from swapping shaders.

This was how the shader was initially configured. It was modified to use
specialization constants because of compilation issues on adreno chips
using Vulkan ([PR](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/pull/161273),
[issue](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/issues/161209)). However,
those chips are now blacklisted from Vulkan
([PR](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/pull/178833)) - so no
compilation issues occur.

The environment set during unification is usually a product of many

and built the masked op with immediate 0.

code. Once Round lowers to VRNDSCALEPS512 [0] next to RoundScaled, the
rule above would rewrite a masked RoundScaled(n) into a masked
RoundScaled(0). Match and keep the immediate.

The S390X rules that narrow 64-bit compares to 32 bits include
(CMPUconst x:(MOV(H|B)reg _) [c]) => (CMPWUconst x [c]). For a negative

immediate, but its low 32 bits can be smaller, so uint64(int8(-128)) <
0xFFFFFFFF folds to true. Restrict that instance to c>=0; the three other
instances (signed compare, or zero-extended value) stay.

cmd/compile: run deadcode before decompose addr

decomposeAddr and mem2reg decide which locals to promote by looking at
every user of the local's address, and any user they cannot model
counts as an escape. Expand calls and decompose builtin leave dead
values behind, and when one of those is a user of a local's address
(an unused SliceMake of a [1]byte temporary's address, say) the local
is rejected for a use that no longer exists. deadcode was only run
after decomposeAddr, so both passes classified against the unswept
function.

Run deadcode once before decompose addr instead. Across std, cmd/go
and cmd/compile this raises decomposeAddr promotions from 11420 to
13146 and mem2reg promotions from 105158 to 108458.

This also retires decomposeAddr's special handling of dead loads: the
wide composite loads that decompose builtin leaves behind after
rewriting their selectors are now gone before the pass looks, so the
candidate loop and the rewrite phase no longer need to step around
them.

net/http/internal/http2: fix/simplify tracking of pending requests

Accounting of an in-flight request can go through various stages:
  - Reserved (not sent, concurrency slot claimed).
  - Pending (waiting for a concurrency slot).
  - Active (sent).

The distinction between "reserved" and "pending" is for two reasons:
A request may be sent without a reservation (moving straight to pending),
and a request with a reservation may still need to wait for a concurrency
slot if the server's concurrency limit changes between the reservation
and the send.

Changes in this CL:

Move a request from "reserved" into "pending" at the start of
the round trip, so all requests are consistently in the same
state (pending) in the interval between the round trip starting
and a stream ID being assigned.

Count pending requests towards the current request count,
and treat connections with pending requests as non-idle.

Add ResizeImagePolicy.cover (#194665)

This PR adds `ResizeImagePolicy.cover`. With this policy, `ResizeImage`
decodes the image at the smallest size that covers the `width` x
`height` box and keeps the aspect ratio of the image, like
`BoxFit.cover`.

### Problem

There is no resize policy that matches `BoxFit.cover`. A caller that
paints with `BoxFit.cover` and does not know the aspect ratio of the
image before the decode has two options:

- Use `ResizeImagePolicy.fit`, or set only one of `cacheWidth` and
`cacheHeight`. For many aspect ratios, the decoded image is smaller than
the box, so it is blurry when it is painted.
- Do not resize. The image is decoded at full size, which uses much more
memory than necessary.

simd/archsimd/_gen/unify: track sum discriminators

Most sums in an environment set are a choice between values of a single
ident: every term binds that ident, either directly or as a factor of a
product. envSet.bind constructs such sums. For example, decoding
"!sum [a, b, c]" creates a variable $sum0 bound by the environment set

	{sum0: a} + {sum0: b} + {sum0: c}

Unification of a variable also constructs such sums, since it binds the
variable in each environment it returns. For example, unifying $sum0
with a value that rules out a returns an environment set of the form

	({sum0: b} ⨯ E₁) + ({sum0: c} ⨯ E₂)

where E₁ and E₂ are the environment sets that result from unifying b
and c with that value.

Record the ident that such a sum chooses between as its "discriminator".
Since the factors of a product bind disjoint idents, a sum binds its
discriminator only in the root factors of its terms. The next CL will
use this to partition these sums without walking the whole environment
set.

Fixed #37255 -- Avoided relying on implicit SELECT ordering in tests.

Many (~70) tests assert a specific row order for querysets whose SQL has no
ORDER BY. SQL standard does not define that order.

On PostgreSQL the rows usually arrive in physical storage order, which
on a freshly loaded table matches insertion order -- so these assertions
pass by coincidence rather than by contract. That breaks when rows are
updated or deleted and the space is reused, or when the planner picks a
different access path such as an index scan. A test like this can start
failing with no change to Django or to the test itself.

cmd/compile: use RVV for RISCV64 LoweredZeroLoop

Use an RVV zeroing loop for large Zero operations on all RISC-V
profiles, with a runtime dispatch on riscv64HasV.

LoweredZeroLoop checks GORISCV64 during code generation. For rva23
and later it emits the RVV loop directly.
For GORISCV64 < rva23, the compiler will emit code with a runtime
check of riscv64HasV for large Zero operations.

The RVV zeroing loop uses V24-V31 as an LMUL=8 group (via VSE8V),
X5 as the remaining byte count, and X6 as the active VL. It sets VL
with AVL=n before the main loop, so the hot loop has no vsetvli; only
a non-empty tail requires a second vsetvli.

### Description

Fixes part of https://github.com/flutter/flutter/issues/182476

When exporting large images via `Picture.toImage()`, Chrome may silently
clamp the physical WebGL drawing buffer during in-place canvas resizing,
leaving pixels outside the clamped area unbacked and producing
transparent strips.

This PR updates `CkOffscreenSurface` to detect when the drawing buffer

the buffer cleanly upfront. If the requested size exceeds what the
browser/GPU can support even after recreation, an `UnsupportedError` is
thrown rather than silently returning clipped pixels.

reflect: document methods affected by CanAddr and CanSet

Addressability (or rather lack of it) is arguably among the most common
causes of panics in Go reflection code
(a contended ranking competing against nil and unexported field panics).

Most Go reflection code knows what exact Go types/kinds it is operating on,
so panics due to mismatching types are rarer (or more easily in code review).
However, whether a value is addressable is determined by the origin of the value,
rather than an intrinsic property of the reflection logic itself.
Thus, knowing whether something is addressable or not is important
to mentally keep track of for correctly written Go reflection code.

A relatively large surface of Value methods are not safe to call
if the value is not addressable. We should explicitly specify
the set of affected methods in CanAddr.

simd/archsimd: optimize unsigned GreaterEqual/LessEqual using min/max

This is purely an optimization; it does not change the API, semantics,
or required CPU features.

On amd64 below AVX512, unsigned GreaterEqual and LessEqual on 8-, 16-,
and 32-bit elements were emulated by flipping the sign bits, using the
signed comparison, and negating the result. For example, for 16-bit
elements:

	VPCMPEQW, VPSLLW (sign-bit constant), VPXOR, VPXOR, VPCMPGTW,
	VPXOR (negate)

Instead, use x >= y iff max(x, y) == x and x <= y iff min(x, y) == x:

	VPMAXUW/VPMINUW, VPCMPEQW

VPMAXU[BWD] and VPMINU[BWD] are AVX at 128 bits and AVX2 at 256
bits, the same as the instructions they replace. 64-bit unsigned
min/max (VPMAXUQ/VPMINUQ) requires AVX512, so 64-bit elements still
use sign flipping.

Link to original PR in automatic cherry-pick PRs (#196130)

When `easy-cp.yml` opens an automatic cherry-pick PR, the generated

doesn't overwrite the link when applying the template.
